data.title: Thailand must halt imminent forcible return of two Uyghur men to China, says Amnesty
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thailand must halt imminent forcible return of two Uyghur men to China, says Amnesty
Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said:
“Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year's unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China.
“These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape.
"Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.
“No amount of diplomatic assurance from China can override Thailand’s obligations not to return anyone to a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations. After more than a decade in detention, these men must be released and given the chance to rebuild their lives in safety and freedom "
Background The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of over 300 who were apprehended without charge by the Thai authorities on 13 March 2014 after they had fled persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

data.title: Thai authorities must not return two Uyghur refugees to China, says Human Rights Watch
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thai authorities must not return two Uyghur refugees to China, says Human Rights Watch
Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today (4 November). The two men, whose names are not public for security reasons, were transferred from prison to immigration detention in Bangkok after receiving a royal pardon, apparently in preparation for deportation.
“Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul should end forced returns to China and allow the two Uyghur men to travel to a safe third country.”
The two Uyghur men have been detained by Thai authorities since 2014, when one of them was only 14 years old. They were serving a prison sentence for offenses related to an escape attempt from immigration detention in January 2020. On October 21, 2026, the authorities transferred them from Bangkok Central Prison to the Bangkok Immigration Detention Center Suan Phlu after they had served most of their seven-year sentence. Thai Foreign Ministry officials told a parliamentary committee that in August the Chinese embassy in Bangkok demanded their return to China.
Under Thai immigration law and regulations, the two Uyghur men will be deported to China unless they object to the deportation and are resettled to a third country. Lawyers representing them told Human Rights Watch that they have already informed Thai authorities that the two do not consent to be sent to China. Thai immigration authorities have repeatedly refused to allow the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) access to the men to determine their refugee status.

data.title: International Court of Justice to rule on 19 November in Myanmar Genocide case
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
International Court of Justice to rule on 19 November in Myanmar Genocide case
The International Court of Justice has announced that it will deliver its judgment on November 19, 2026, in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Genocide Convention, Human Rights Watch said today in releasing a question-and-answer document on key issues in the case.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the International Court of Justice alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. This is not a criminal case against individuals, but a request for a legal determination of Myanmar’s state responsibility for genocide.
“The International Court of Justice’s Myanmar judgment will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya’s quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling will also be a stark reminder that the oppression of the Rohingya is ongoing, and that rights-respecting countries need to act decisively to support them, promote justice for atrocities, and ensure their safe and voluntary return.”
The judgment, which is final with no possibility to appeal, will conclude the proceedings in this case before the court.

data.title: Two Thai opposition MPs warned their phones have been targeted by spyware
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Two Thai opposition MPs warned their phones have been targeted by spyware
Leaders of the People’s Party and Democrat Party have revealed that their phones may have been compromised by the sophisticated Pegasus spyware after Apple issued the latest round of notifications to victims. The same warning was given following the 2020 mass protests when Thai pro-democracy activists, journalists, politicians and academics were notified of being the targets of state-sponsored attacks.
MP Abhisit Vejjajiva, leader of the opposition Democrat Party, revealed on Monday (2 November) that his phone received a notification from Apple saying that his phone was targeted by a highly sophisticated surveillance spyware. On Tuesday (3 November), Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, leader of the opposition People’s Party, revealed that he received the same notification, according to iLaw.
It is noticeable that the notifications came ahead of the upcoming no-confidence debate on 7-11 December and coincided with the opposition’s preparations to scrutinise the government, particularly over the Senate selection fraud. It remain unclear at this time who is responsible for the attacks.
Apple issued the latest round of threat notifications in late October to iPhone users who may have been targeted by mercenary spyware.
According to public reporting and research by civil society organizations, technology firms, and journalists, individually targeted attacks have historically been associated with state actors, including private companies developing mercenary spyware on their behalf, such as Pegasus from the Israeli NSO Group.
The Pegasus spyware can infiltrate a target’s device without the use of clickbait lures employed in other hacks, and an automatic tracking record erasure that removes software footprints. It allows attackers to gain complete control over an infected phone, providing access to photos, videos, messages and call records. data.title: Gathering marks 20th anniversary of anti-coup suicide
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Gathering marks 20th anniversary of anti-coup suicide
Photo: Ginger Cat
On Saturday (31 October), a gathering took place at an overpass on Vibhavadi Road to mark the 20th anniversary of the death of Nuamthong Praiwan, a taxi driver who crashed his taxi into a tank and later took his own life in protest of the 19 September 2006 military coup.
Activists, politicians, and members of the public participated in the gathering, which started at around 12.30 with live music, followed by a Buddhist merit-making ceremony. Flowers were placed around the overpass.
The rapper Elevenfinger also performed at the gathering. Before the event ended, former Red Shirt leader Thida Tavornseth led the participants in making a pledge to push for a new Constitution in line with the result of the 2026 referendum and for the repeal of laws that are relics of military coups.
After the coup, on 30 September 2006, Nuamthong crashed his taxi into a tank parked near the Equestrian Statue of King Chulalongkorn to protest the coup. He was seriously injured..
On 31 October 2006, Nuamthong was found hanging from the overpass in front of the Thairath newspaper office on Vibhavadi Road. He had committed suicide after Akkara Thairoj, a deputy spokesperson for the military junta, expressed scepticism about his intentions by asserting that “nobody’s ideals are so great that they would sacrifice their lives for them.”
Nuamthong’s suicide note says that he voluntarily crashed his taxi and took his own life and that he dies to demand democracy, and that his suicide is also a response to Akkara’s insult. He also wrote that “I hope that in my next life, there shall be no more coups.”

data.title: Thailand must not return detained Uyghur refugees to China, say rights groups
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thailand must not return detained Uyghur refugees to China, say rights groups
A network of human rights organizations have called on the Thai government not to forcibly return two detained Uyghur refugees to China and to facilitate their resettlement in a third country.
In a joint statement, the Coalition for the Rights of Refugees and Stateless Persons (CRSP), Migrant Working Group (MWG) and Thailand Migration Reform Consortium (TMR) raised concerns about potential forced return to China of two Uyghur refugees detained at the Suan Phlu Immigration Dentetion Centre. The groups said that the two refugees have been detained since 2014 and were moved to immigration detention from prison on 21 October. They have told their legal representatives they do not consent to return to China, but their representatives have not been allowed to see them since their transfer.
The groups noted that, days after the two were moved to immigration detention, the Chinese ambassador to Thailand met the Secretary-General of the National Security Council (NSC). They are now concerned that the NSC may decide whether to return the two refugees to China in an upcoming meeting. They noted that a decision made by the NSC led to the deportation of 40 Uyghur refugees to China, and that none of the 40 refugees could be contacted to confirm their safety.
They call on the Thai government to stop the forced return to Uyghur refugees to China and to facilitate their resettlement in a third country in line with their wishes and that of the receiving country. The Thai government must allow legal representatives, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to access and protect the Uyghur refugees held in immigration detention. It must also respect the free and informed decisions of the two Uyghur refugees.

data.title: Politically connected security companies enabled slavery and rape in scamming compounds in Cambodia, says Amnesty's new report
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Politically connected security companies enabled slavery and rape in scamming compounds in Cambodia, says Amnesty's new report
Cambodian private security companies connected to the country’s military, police and powerful business networks have helped sustain a scamming industry built on trafficking, forced labour, torture and slavery, Amnesty International said in a new report published today (29 October).
Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia identifies five private security companies that provided services at scamming compounds – and details their links to members of Cambodia’s military, police and business elites. Amnesty also identified multiple members of the military and police who worked as security guards, trained or supervised guards at more than 20 compounds.
“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“This report demonstrates Cambodian corporate actors’ direct involvement in scamming compounds. Our findings also begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny.
“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

data.title: iLaw director petitions court for dismissal of PM’s lawsuit
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
iLaw director petitions court for dismissal of PM’s lawsuit
iLaw director Yingcheep Atchanont has filed a petition with the Chief Justice of the Criminal Court requesting that the lawsuit filed against him by Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul be dismissed on the grounds that the case was brought in bad faith.
Anutin filed a defamation lawsuit against Yingcheep over a press conference on 21 July, in which Yingcheep alleged that Anutin was involved with the Senate selection fraud. The press conference came after he filed a petition with the opposition whip calling for an investigation into nine politicians for their alleged involvement in the selection fraud.
Yingcheep’s petition to the Chief Justice of the Criminal Court states that the lawsuit was brought in bad faith and should be dismissed without the need for a preliminary hearing in line with Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a court to dismiss a lawsuit brought in bad faith or those brought in order to harass or take advantage of the defendant. He also cited a recommendation made by the President of the Supreme Court, which states that Section 161 includes lawsuits stemming from campaigns or expression of opinions for the protection of human rights, natural resources and the environment, consumer rights, labour rights, or other public interests, as well as those stemming from the disclosure of information concerning corruption or unlawful conduct.
The petition notes that the information Yingcheep disclosed came from an investigation report compiled by a government agency and is not baseless, while the press conference was held so that relevant agencies would take action without further delay. He also said that it is in the public interest to call for an investigation into the alleged fraud. data.title: Human Rights Foundation condemns sentencing of Anon Nampa
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Human Rights Foundation condemns sentencing of Anon Nampa
The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) has issued a statement condemning the sentencing of human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to an additional 2 years and 8 months in prison on a royal defamation charge and calls for the unconditional and immediate release of Anon and other prisoners of conscience. On 30 October Anon and four other activists were found guilty of royal defamation over speeches given at a protest on 25 November 2020 and sentenced to 2 years and 8 months in prison. Anon is now facing a cumulative prison sentence of 34 years and 5 months. According to Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR), 33 people are currently detained on a royal defamation charge, 12 of whom are detained pending trial or appeal. The full statement reads: HRF strongly condemns the Thai court’s sentencing of human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to an additional two years and eight months in prison under the country’s royal defamation law (Article 112 of the Criminal Code) for criticizing the monarchy, bringing his total prison sentence to more than 34 years.
Anon is among more than 290 people who have been charged under the royal defamation law since the youth-led protests that began in 2020. He was among the first prominent figures to publicly challenge the longstanding taboo surrounding discussion of the monarchy in Thai https://ow.ly/cc6p5103VJq
The Thai regime has increasingly weaponized the royal defamation law to suppress freedom of dissent. Dozens remain detained, while others have been forced into exile. According to HRF's Tyranny Tracker, Thailand is ruled by a hybrid authoritarian regime, with civic space continuing to shrink. https://ow.ly/gifF5103VJp
HRF calls on the Thai regime for the unconditional and immediate release of Arnon Nampa and other prisoners of conscience. HRF also calls on Thailand to repeal Article 112 of the Criminal Code and bring its practices in line with international human rights law. See less

data.title: Appeal Court dismisses chicken farm company’s lawsuit against human rights defenders
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Appeal Court dismisses chicken farm company’s lawsuit against human rights defenders
The Appeal Court has dismissed a defamation lawsuit filed by the chicken farm company Thammakaset against three human rights defenders for social media posts about abuse of migrant workers at its farm.
The company filed criminal defamation complaints in 2019 against Angkhana Neelapaijit, Puttanee Kangkun, and Thanaporn Saleephol for sharing and posting on social media in support of migrant workers who reported poor working conditions and other human rights defenders who had been sued by the company.
In August 2023, the South Bangkok Criminal Court dismissed the lawsuit on the grounds that the posts were not about the company but expressed support for other advocates being sued by the company, while a video linked to the posts was found in another case to not be defamatory.
According to the Community Resource Centre Foundation (CRC), the Appeal Court ruled on 2 November to uphold the dismissal on the grounds that the defendants were exercising their right to freedom of expression about a public issue and defending human rights. It noted that the posts were not defamatory towards the company and that the business losses that the company claimed were not a direct result of the posts.
The lawsuits against Angkhana, Puttanee, and Thanaporn are among the over 30 civil and criminal cases filed by the company against human rights defenders, journalists, and workers since 2016 after 14 migrant workers from Myanmar submitted a petition to the National Human Rights Commission claiming that they were made to work for wages that were below-he legal minimum without overtime pay and that their documents had been confiscated by their employer.
The workers were sued by the company in October 2019 for defamation, but later acquitted.
